source.title: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis — Technical Summary (IPCC AR6 WGI)
source.rights_status: Reuse and redistribution rights for the downloaded PDF and derived content were not verified; source and generated data remain local and excluded from Git.

questions.question: In Table TS.1, what is identified as the main driver of tropospheric warming since 1979?
questions.gold_answer: Human influence is identified as the main driver.

evidence.region: Table TS.1, row 'Warming of the troposphere since 1979', Human Contribution Assessment column
evidence.supports: The assessment cell says 'Main driver'.

questions.question: In Table TS.2, how do agricultural and ecological drought changes at +1.5°C compare with observed changes?
questions.gold_answer: They increase in more regions than the observed changes.

evidence.region: Table TS.2, 'Agricultural and ecological droughts: Intensity and/or frequency' row, +1.5°C column
evidence.supports: The cell says increases occur in more regions compared with observed changes.

questions.question: In Table TS.3, what is the 50th-percentile remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.7°C?
questions.gold_answer: 850 GtCO2, starting from 1 January 2020.

evidence.region: Table TS.3, row 1.7°C in the 'Global surface temperature change since 1850–1900' column and 50th-percentile TCRE column
evidence.supports: The row is 0.63°C since 2010–2019 / 1.7°C since 1850–1900 and the 50th percentile is 850 GtCO2.

questions.question: Which four water-cycle variables are mapped in Box TS.6, Figure 1?
questions.gold_answer: Precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, and surface soil moisture.

evidence.region: Box TS.6, Figure 1, four map headings
evidence.supports: The maps are labeled precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, and surface soil moisture.

questions.question: In the Figure TS.12(a) mechanisms diagram, name any two labeled factors that contribute to enhanced Mediterranean warming.
questions.gold_answer: Examples include a warm Atlantic Ocean, reduction of aerosols, surface drying, and lapse-rate differences that produce stronger warming over land than over sea.

evidence.region: Figure TS.12(a), schematic 'Mechanisms of enhanced Mediterranean warming'
evidence.supports: The schematic labels the warm Atlantic Ocean, reduction of aerosols, surface drying, and lapse-rate difference.

questions.question: What concept does the upper-left schematic in Figure TS.6 depict?
questions.gold_answer: The likelihood distribution for equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS), including its likely range and low-likelihood tails.

evidence.region: Figure TS.6, upper-left panel
evidence.supports: The panel is labeled 'Schematic ECS likelihood' and shows relative likelihood against ECS.

questions.question: In Figure TS.2, what are the three plotted dimensions that show progress in climate models?
questions.gold_answer: Model resolution, model complexity, and representation of key variables; panel (c) evaluates the latter using pattern correlation with observational references.

evidence.region: Figure TS.2 panels (a), (b), and (c)
evidence.supports: The caption identifies progress in resolution, complexity, and representation of key variables; panel (c) is labeled pattern correlation with observational reference.

questions.question: In Figure TS.3, what warming level is used to show the historical temperature-change and signal-to-noise patterns?
questions.gold_answer: A global warming level of 1°C.

evidence.region: Figure TS.3 caption and panels (a) and (b)
evidence.supports: The caption says the observed temperature change and signal-to-noise ratio are shown at a 1°C global warming level.

questions.question: In Figure TS.9(a), over what time span are proxy-record carbon-dioxide changes shown?
questions.gold_answer: Over the past 3.5 million years.

evidence.region: Figure TS.9(a), x- and y-axes
evidence.supports: The Figure TS.9 caption says panel (a) shows proxy-record CO2 changes over the past 3.5 million years.

questions.question: Figure TS.13 covers the 1971–2018 energy-budget period. Combining the accompanying text with that figure, what expected energy gain is estimated from the likely ERF range and central radiative-response estimate?
questions.gold_answer: For 1971–2018, 340 ZJ, with a range of 47–662 ZJ.

evidence.region: Figure TS.13 caption and panel (f)
evidence.supports: The figure concerns net cumulative energy change for 1971–2018 and identifies the energy-budget panel.

evidence.region: Paragraph beginning 'Improved quantifications of ERF...'
evidence.supports: The expected energy gain is 340 [47 to 662] ZJ.

questions.question: What does Table TS.1 report as the human contribution to ocean heat-content increase, and which two indicators are plotted in Figure TS.11?
questions.gold_answer: Table TS.1 identifies human influence as the main driver; Figure TS.11 includes marine heatwaves and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC).

evidence.region: Table TS.1, Ocean heat content increase since the 1970s row, Human Contribution Assessment column
evidence.supports: The cell says 'Main driver'.

evidence.region: Figure TS.11 panels
evidence.supports: The figure includes marine heatwaves and AMOC indicators.

questions.question: Relative to what baseline are global warming levels expressed in the prose, and how is the Figure TS.6 heat-warning index measured?
questions.gold_answer: GWLs are relative to 1850–1900; the heat-warning index is the average number of days per year that the NOAA Heat Index reaches the 'danger' level for human health.

evidence.region: Prose describing global warming levels
evidence.supports: The report defines GWLs relative to 1850–1900.

evidence.region: Figure TS.6 caption, heat-warning-index description
evidence.supports: The index is average days per year at which the NOAA Heat Index reaches the human-health 'danger' level.

questions.question: What does the Technical Summary say about the near-term global-warming effect of changes in short-lived climate forcers across scenarios?
questions.gold_answer: Changes in short-lived climate forcers will very likely cause further warming over the next two decades across all scenarios.

evidence.region: Selected Updates and/or New Results Since AR5, SRCCL and SROCC, short-lived climate forcers bullet
evidence.supports: The text says changes in SLCFs will very likely cause further warming in the next two decades across all scenarios.

questions.question: What CH4 concentration and increase since 1750 does the summary report for 2019?
questions.gold_answer: 1,866.3 ± 3.3 ppb, an increase of 1,137 ± 10 ppb since 1750.

evidence.region: Paragraph beginning 'By 2019, concentrations of CH4 reached...'
evidence.supports: The paragraph reports 1,866.3 (±3.3) ppb and an increase since 1750 of 1,137 ± 10 ppb.

questions.question: According to the summary, how did the temporary emissions reductions associated with COVID-19 containment affect radiative forcing and detectability of climate responses?
questions.gold_answer: They produced a small positive net radiative effect (warming influence), but global and regional climate responses were undetectable above internal variability because the emissions reductions were temporary.

evidence.region: COVID-19 bullet under Selected Updates and/or New Results Since AR5, SRCCL and SROCC
evidence.supports: The text describes a small positive net radiative effect and undetectable global and regional responses above internal variability.

questions.question: According to this Technical Summary, what was the EU ETS allowance price in euros per tonne on 1 January 2030?
questions.absence_check: Checked the full extracted text and indexed visual/table content for EU ETS allowance prices and 2030 price forecasts; the report does not provide that market-price datum.

questions.question: What was Hanoi's population in 2020 according to this Technical Summary?
questions.absence_check: Checked the full report text, tables, and visual descriptions for Hanoi population data; no city-population statistic is reported.

questions.question: What exact carbon-tax rate does this Technical Summary recommend for Canada in 2030?
questions.absence_check: Checked the full report for a Canadian carbon-tax recommendation or rate; the Technical Summary does not specify one.

questions.question: In Table TS.2, how does the frequency or intensity of cold extremes change at both +2°C and +4°C global warming?
questions.gold_answer: It decreases at both warming levels.

evidence.region: Table TS.2, 'Cold extremes: Frequency or intensity' row, +2°C and +4°C columns
evidence.supports: Both projected cells contain a downward arrow.

questions.question: Table TS.2 gives what projected change in the proportion of intense tropical cyclones at +4°C?
questions.gold_answer: An increase of 20%.

evidence.region: Table TS.2, 'Tropical cyclones: Proportion of intense cyclones' row, +4°C column
evidence.supports: The +4°C cell says increase +20%.

questions.question: At +2°C, what change in the rate of precipitation associated with tropical cyclones is shown in Table TS.2?
questions.gold_answer: An increase of 14%.

evidence.region: Table TS.2, 'Precipitation associated with tropical cyclones' row, +2°C column
evidence.supports: The +2°C cell says rate +14%.

questions.question: What change in co-occurring heatwaves and droughts is projected as global warming increases, according to Table TS.2?
questions.gold_answer: Their frequency and intensity increase with warming.

evidence.region: Table TS.2, 'Compound events: Co-occurrent heatwaves and droughts' row, projected +1.5°C cell
evidence.supports: The cell states frequency and intensity increase with warming.

questions.question: In Table TS.3, what is the 50th-percentile remaining carbon budget for a 1.8°C warming limit?
questions.gold_answer: 1,000 GtCO2, starting from 1 January 2020.

evidence.region: Table TS.3, 1.8°C row and 50th-percentile TCRE column
evidence.supports: The value is 1,000 GtCO2.

questions.question: In Table TS.3, what is the 50th-percentile remaining carbon budget for a 1.9°C warming limit?
questions.gold_answer: 1,200 GtCO2, starting from 1 January 2020.

evidence.region: Table TS.3, 1.9°C row and 50th-percentile TCRE column
evidence.supports: The value is 1,200 GtCO2.

questions.question: What major stages does Figure TS.4 show between anthropogenic emissions and regional climatic impact-drivers?
questions.gold_answer: Emissions lead to atmospheric concentrations, radiative forcing, global climate change/warming, and ultimately regional climate change and climatic impact-drivers.

evidence.region: Figure TS.4, central cause–effect chain and caption
evidence.supports: The diagram and caption show the emissions → concentrations → forcing → global climate → regional climate/impact-driver sequence.

questions.question: Which three variables are mapped in Figure TS.5(b) across global warming levels?
questions.gold_answer: Near-surface air temperature, precipitation, and soil moisture.

evidence.region: Figure TS.5(b), three map-column headings
evidence.supports: The map columns are temperature change, precipitation change, and soil moisture change.

questions.question: In Figure TS.14, what three stages follow the baseline top-of-atmosphere energy budget after a perturbation?
questions.gold_answer: Instantaneous changes to the radiation balance, adjustments to meteorology and composition, and feedback responses.

evidence.region: Figure TS.14 sequence across panels (a)–(d)
evidence.supports: The schematic labels instantaneous changes, adjustments, and feedback responses after the baseline.

questions.question: In Figure TS.21, which region and season are used for the illustrated precipitation case study?
questions.gold_answer: South-Eastern South America (SES), during austral summer (DJF).

evidence.region: Figure TS.21 title and panel (a) heading
evidence.supports: The case study is South-Eastern South America and the precipitation is austral summer (DJF).

questions.question: Figure TS.23 compares which two observational datasets, and what do grey regions mean on the CRUTEM5 map?
questions.gold_answer: Berkeley Earth and CRUTEM5; grey means there are not enough data (less than 50% of the region is covered by available data).

evidence.region: Figure TS.23 map labels and caption
evidence.supports: The upper and lower maps use Berkeley Earth and CRUTEM5; the caption says grey CRUTEM5 regions have data over less than 50% of the area.

questions.question: Which two SSP scenario trajectories are plotted in Figure TS.5(a)?
questions.gold_answer: SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0.

evidence.region: Figure TS.5(a), legend and caption
evidence.supports: The chart shows CMIP6 simulations for SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0.

questions.question: In Figure TS.12(b), what does the horizontal axis measure, and what two outcomes are shown for 10-year and 50-year heavy-precipitation events?
questions.gold_answer: The horizontal axis is global surface temperature change relative to 1850–1900; the chart shows relative event frequency and intensity change (in percent) for 10-year and 50-year heavy-precipitation events.

evidence.region: Figure TS.12(b), axes, legend, and caption
evidence.supports: The x-axis is global temperature change since 1850–1900; the panel plots relative frequency and intensity for 10- and 50-year heavy precipitation events.

questions.question: What five emissions-stage labels are shown in Figure TS.19?
questions.gold_answer: Large net positive CO2 emissions, small net positive CO2 emissions, two net-negative CO2-emissions stages (the second is marked as a period with no significant change), and net zero CO2 emissions and removals.

evidence.region: Figure TS.19 chart labels (a)–(e)
evidence.supports: The five chart stages are explicitly labeled in the figure.

questions.question: What period and unit does Figure TS.13 use for its net cumulative energy-change estimates?
questions.gold_answer: The period is 1971–2018 and the unit is ZJ, where 1 ZJ equals 10^21 joules.

evidence.region: Figure TS.13 caption and panel labels
evidence.supports: The caption states 1971–2018 and defines ZJ as 10^21 joules.

questions.question: In Figure TS.11, name two ocean or cryosphere indicators for which past and future changes are shown.
questions.gold_answer: Examples include marine heatwaves, AMOC, dissolved oxygen, and ocean acidification.

evidence.region: Figure TS.11 panels and caption
evidence.supports: The figure includes chart panels for marine heatwaves, AMOC, dissolved oxygen, and ocean acidification.

questions.question: What cause–effect sequence does Figure TS.4 show from emissions to climatic impact-drivers, and what change in the proportion of intense tropical cyclones does Table TS.2 project at +4°C?
questions.gold_answer: Emissions lead to atmospheric concentrations, radiative forcing, global climate change, and regional climate change/climatic impact-drivers; the proportion of intense tropical cyclones increases by 20% at +4°C.

evidence.region: Figure TS.4 cause–effect chain
evidence.supports: The figure connects emissions and forcing to regional climate and climatic impact-drivers.

evidence.region: Table TS.2, proportion of intense tropical cyclones row, +4°C column
evidence.supports: The +4°C cell reports an increase of 20%.

questions.question: For a 1.5°C limit, Table TS.3 gives the 50th-percentile remaining carbon budget. How much larger would the budget be if AR5-era evidence and methods were used instead?
questions.gold_answer: The Table TS.3 budget is 500 GtCO2; using AR5-era evidence and methods would make the 1.5°C budget about 300–350 GtCO2 larger.

evidence.region: Table TS.3, 1.5°C row, 50th-percentile TCRE column
evidence.supports: The remaining budget is 500 GtCO2 from 1 January 2020.

evidence.region: Paragraph comparing AR6 budgets with AR5 methods
evidence.supports: The 1.5°C budget would be about 300–350 GtCO2 larger with AR5-era evidence and methods.

questions.question: Figure TS.21 identifies drivers of the South-Eastern South America precipitation trend. Using the figure and the accompanying prose, name three modes of variability and the external forcing influences mentioned.
questions.gold_answer: The modes include AMV, ENSO, and PDV; the external influences include greenhouse-gas increases, ozone depletion, and aerosols.

evidence.region: Figure TS.21(a), labeled driver diagram
evidence.supports: The diagram labels AMV, ENSO, PDV, GHG plus O3 depletion, and Aerosol.

evidence.region: Paragraph beginning 'Austral summer (DJF) precipitation positive trends...'
evidence.supports: The text names AMV, ENSO, and PDV, along with GHG increases and ozone depletion together with aerosols.

questions.question: Table TS.4 says what about human influence on observed ENSO changes, and what percentages of Northern Central America interannual SAT and precipitation variance are explained by ENSO?
questions.gold_answer: There is low agreement on human influence; ENSO explains 13% of SAT variance and 27% of precipitation variance in Northern Central America.

evidence.region: Table TS.4(a), Human influence on observed changes row, ENSO column
evidence.supports: The cell says 'Low agreement'.

evidence.region: Table TS.4(b), Northern Central America row, ENSO DJF SAT and precipitation columns
evidence.supports: The ENSO values are 13% for SAT and 27% for precipitation.

questions.question: What range of CO2 release from permafrost do the cited models project per 1°C of global warming by 2100?
questions.gold_answer: 3–41 PgC per 1°C of global warming by 2100.

evidence.region: Paragraph beginning 'Thawing terrestrial permafrost will lead to carbon release...'
evidence.supports: The ensemble projects CO2 release of 3–41 PgC per 1°C by 2100.

questions.question: What was identified as the main driver of upper-stratospheric cooling since 1979?
questions.gold_answer: Stratospheric ozone depletion due to ozone-depleting substances.

evidence.region: Paragraph discussing stratospheric cooling
evidence.supports: The text identifies ozone depletion due to ozone-depleting substances as the main driver of upper-stratospheric cooling since 1979.

questions.question: Why are single-model initial-condition large ensembles needed in the regional climate discussion?
questions.gold_answer: They are needed to separate internal variability from forced changes and to partition sources of uncertainty across future assessed periods.

evidence.region: Paragraph beginning 'In addition, single-model initial-condition large ensembles...'
evidence.supports: The text states both purposes.

questions.question: Which two physical contributions underpin the AR6 global mean sea-level projections described in the summary?
questions.gold_answer: Ocean thermal expansion and land-ice contributions.

evidence.region: Projected global mean sea level change bullet under TS.1
evidence.supports: The text says projections are based on ocean thermal expansion and land-ice contribution estimates.
